Stubble management is a significant issue in Western Australia particularly in the high rainfall zone, where it is not uncommon for cereal yields to reach over 7 t/ha with the resulting stubble loads being up to 10 t/ha. This is a high amount of stubble residue left post harvest and is an increasing concern for local growers due to poor establishment of following crops, nitrogen (N) tie-up, disease carryover issues and seeding operation inefficiencies such as, blockages, hair pinning, poor soil throw and bulldozing. As a result, plant establishment has become increasingly difficult, particularly Canola establishment.  Traditionally, high stubble loads in the region have been removed by burning, however, there has been a move away from burning due to a combination of social license issues, as well as farming system concerns. Burning increases the risk of erosion and nutrient loss and decreases soil moisture. Growers are also concerned with Nitrogen (N) tie-up from retained crop stubble. Although cereal stubbles contribute very little N to the following crop, stubbles are a source of carbon and N is required from the soil to breakdown this high carbon material. Previous GRDC research has been conducted to understand the additional N requirements needed to overcome early N immobilisation by stubble, this research suggests that an additional 5-6 kg N/t of cereal residue can help overcome the issues of stubble N immobilisation. (https://grdc.com.au/resources-and-publications/grdc-update-papers/tab-content/grdc-update-papers/2018/02/the-effect-of-stubble-on-nitrogen-tie-up-and-supply). Investigation into whether the addition of nutrients, in addition to an enzyme ‘digester’ to stubble in conjunction with mechanical stubble treatments, during the summer fallow period, can increase the rate of stubble breakdown to allow for improved winter crop establishment (especially canola) and reduction in early season nitrogen tie-up. Reduced carryover of stubble-borne diseases could also be explored via observations

A review of the final report from FAR2403-001SAX NGN- Winter wheat investigation on the Southcoast of WA has presented a number of questions with local growers in the Albany Port Zone to investigate earlier sowing times for commercially available winter wheat varieties. Results from the previous investment highlighted some interesting trends regarding the contribution of grain from secondary tillers in both winter wheat varieties and spring barley varieties. There is a need to continue this investigation over a 2-year period to determine if this is a common occurrence. With the trend continuing towards earlier sowing dates to either satisfy large hectare programs or to take advantage of late summer rainfall utilising some winter wheat varieties as an addition to more common spring wheat varieties could allow growers to take advantage of the conditions when they can. There is also a need to provide comparisons between different cereal crops including barley and oats to provide rotational diversity in the area.

Local growers report a yield ceiling in oats, unlike barley, suggesting a challenge in achieving higher grain yield. This may stem from higher biomass and a source-sink imbalance, making oats more vulnerable to environmental stress. Last season’s trials support this, showing excessive nitrogen reduced harvest index and grain weight, ultimately lowering yields—likely due to increased biomass and greater susceptibility to terminal drought (data available on request).   Further reinforcing this, trials showed significantly higher yields when oats were planted in late March instead of late April, suggesting early seeding helps mitigate drought effects. Overseas research also links vegetative indices (multispectral analysis) at panicle emergence and early grain fill to final yield, suggesting these indices could serve as a tool for identifying unrealized yield potential.   By comparing up to 3 milling oats varieties that with difference in phenology and crop architecture this research will seek to address the following issues:     * Maximise oat yield, quality and profit through efficient use of nitrogen.   * Provide insights into the relationship between time of sowing, biomass growth, nitrogen application, and grain yield in oats.   * Identify whether variety specific characteristics offer opportunities to overcome the yield ceiling.   * Identify the risk (lack of photoperiod hold) or benefits (grain yield) with early seeding of varieties.   * Use multispectral technology to improve decision-making tools for growers.   * Contribute to sustainable oat production by addressing yield limitations associated with excessive vegetative growth, terminal drought, and over-fertilization.   Trials are to be applied to farmer-sown strips of up to 3 milling oats varieties that with difference in phenology and crop architecture (4 randomized replicates within each block). A range of environments to capture N response & rainfall/terminal drought influence: 1. Low Rainfall (Lake Grace): 4N rates, 2 TOS, 3 varieties (96 plots) 2. Medium Rainfall (Narrogin): 4N rates, 2 TOS, 3 varieties (96 plots) 3. High Rainfall (Williams): 5N rates, 1 TOS, 3 varieties (60 plots)

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority oversees herbicide registration, requiring extensive trials to ensure crop safety and efficacy. However, due to the high cost of testing across Australia’s diverse conditions, not all soil types and climates are comprehensively covered. Registrants typically focus on environments representing the majority of the market, leaving smaller, atypical environments untested. Growers in these regions must often learn through experience, particularly with pre-emergent herbicides, which are more prone to challenges in lighter sandy soils and soils altered by amelioration practices such as claying and delving/mixing.   Stakeholder meetings have highlighted several issues with new pre-emergent herbicides, including yield losses, crop damage, and inconsistent weed control. In some cases, herbicide efficacy varies significantly across different soil types, while residues have been found to affect crop safety. Inadequate label information has also contributed to these challenges, with growers expressing concerns about poor communication from chemical companies regarding product performance and risks. In the Western and Southern regions, significant crop damage has been observed in sandy soils, along with complications related to plant-back intervals. In the Northern and Southern regions, growers have reported herbicide efficacy and safety issues in alkaline soils. The consultancy report and stakeholders involved in ULA2402-003CAX identified the evaluation of climatic, soil, and management factors affecting the efficacy and crop safety of major pre-emergent and post-emergent herbicides as a top research priority.

Growers and advisers in the Western Region have raised concerns about nitrogen management, identifying it as a critical issue in multiple stakeholder forums. Feedback has highlighted the need for effective strategies that allow growers to optimise nitrogen use, reduce costs, and minimise environmental impact, all tailored to their specific farming systems, soil types, and environmental conditions. This project aims to address these challenges by optimising nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in the Geraldton Port Zone, with the goal of improving both economic viability and environmental sustainability in farming practices. Building on similar projects in the Western Region, the initiative will focus on developing practical, evidence-based guidelines to support informed decision-making regarding nitrogen use. It will draw on data and insights from previous and current industry and GRDC-led projects, expanding through the collection of new data from existing and additional trial sites. The findings from these trials will inform the creation of clear, actionable guidelines to help growers optimise nitrogen use, adapt to seasonal variations, and correctly use monitoring tools for informed decision-making on nitrogen application. Ultimately, the goal is to reduce nitrogen-related costs, enhance nitrogen efficiency, and improve farm productivity, all while considering environmental sustainability, particularly regarding nitrogen losses and fertiliser use. To ensure effective adoption, the project will include targeted extension activities to communicate the findings and support growers in implementing these practices, ultimately leading to improved NUE.

Scarab infestations have been an ongoing concern for growers, particularly in the Lakes and Kondinin regions, where root and crown feeding has led to significant crop damage and failures. Though sporadic, outbreaks have resulted in substantial yield losses. More recently, barley crops in the Great Southern Agricultural Region have also been affected, with some paddocks experiencing 5-6% plant loss due to persistent larval feeding. Effective management of scarabs is complicated by the diversity of species, each with distinct life cycles, behaviours, and responses to control measures. Accurate species identification is critical, as some larvae remain below the soil surface-rendering contact insecticides ineffective-while others are beneficial and should not be targeted. Additionally, growers face increasing restrictions on chemical control options, including the loss of chlorpyrifos. Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides contributes to resistance development and harms beneficial insect populations through off-target effects. Preliminary analysis by DPIRD on scarabs collected from Lake Grace found no genetic matches in GenBank or Bold databases, suggesting the presence of previously undescribed species. This discovery led to a variation within the NGDSI (DPIRD) project to: 1    Develop molecular characterisation techniques for identifying cockchafers across all life stages. 2    Map the potential distribution of key species across WA. 3    Focus management strategies on species that are complex ground occupiers. This project will build on and complement the NGDSI variation by bridging species identification with practical pest management solutions. While the NGDSI work focuses on refining molecular tools and mapping species distribution, this project will develop targeted management strategies-including chemical and agronomic approaches-tailored to the specific scarab species present in key hotspots such as Lake Grace and Kondinin. By linking species-level insights with actionable control measures, these efforts will provide growers with integrated, evidence-based tools to mitigate scarab damage, enhance crop protection, and reduce reliance on ineffective chemical treatments, ultimately supporting more sustainable and effective pest management across WA's agricultural regions.

GrainData Fusion: Leveraging INVITA datasets to enhance their utility for new analytics tasks
Environmental Accounting Platform Communication and Adoption Program

Western Australian grain growers are challenged by a changing climate, shifting rainfall later in the cropping season (Green, et al., 2025). The importance of understanding what crop to grow when soil moisture is minimal, and no significant rainfall event occurs until after May, is vital for grain growers to maximise profit.   In the Geraldton port zone, the average season break is the 22nd of May (Guthrie pers. comms.), prompting growers to conduct dry seeding prior to the break of season. Dry seeding, however, can lead to challenges such as compromised seeding depth, reduced herbicide effectiveness and sub-optimal furrow formation. It also carries risks like false breaks that may result in increased seedling mortality. Conversely, delaying seeding until after the break can enhance weed management (offering benefit of double knock herbicide strategies), provide confidence in soil moisture availability, and improve furrow structure.   Other research has investigated timing of sowing across different cultivars, which has ultimately informed the practice of early sowing, however, these findings have failed to address scenarios where late sowing is the only option, particularly as a result of a late break – a scenario which may become more frequent in the Geraldton port zone due to changing climatic conditions.

Cancer Australia has executed a contract with the University of Technology, as represented by the Cancer Quality of Life Expert Service Team (CQUEST), as the supplier for the Quality of Life (QoL) National Technical Service (NTS). CQUEST will provide Multi-site Collaborative Cancer Clinical Trials Groups with expert advice and support for the inclusion of Health-related Quality of Life (HRQOL) and Patient Reported Outcomes (PRO) measures and/or sub-studies into investigator-initiated and industry-independent cancer clinical trial concepts and protocols for the period 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2027.

Cancer Australia has executed a contract with the University of Technology, as represented by the Centre for Health Economics Research and Evaluation (CHERE) as the supplier for the Health- and Pharmaco-economics (HE) National Technical Service (NTS). CHERE will provide Multi-site Collaborative Cancer Clinical Trials Groups with expert advice and support for the inclusion of HE measures/sub-studies into investigator-initiated and industry-independent cancer clinical trial concepts and protocols for the period 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2027.

WA grain growers are challenged by a changing climate, shifting rainfall later in the cropping season (Green, et alk 2025).  The importance of understanding what crop to grow when soil moisture is minimal, and no significant rainfall event occurs until after May, is vital for grain growers to maximise profit.

This project will build on and complement the NGDSI variation by bridging species identification with practical pest management solutions. While the NGDSI work focuses on refining molecular tools and mapping species distribution, this project will develop targeted management strategies—including chemical and agronomic approaches—tailored to the specific scarab species present in key hotspots such as Lake Grace and Kondinin. By linking species-level insights with actionable control measures, these efforts will provide growers with integrated, evidence-based tools to mitigate scarab damage, enhance crop protection, and reduce reliance on ineffective chemical treatments, ultimately supporting more sustainable and effective pest management across WA’s agricultural regions.

Local growers report a yield ceiling in oats, unlike barley, suggesting a challenge in achieving higher grain yield. This may stem from higher biomass and a source-sink imbalance, making oats more vulnerable to environmental stress. Last season’s trials support this, showing excessive nitrogen reduced harvest index and grain weight, ultimately lowering yields—likely due to increased biomass and greater susceptibility to terminal drought.

During the 2024 season outbreaks of flag smut in wheat and loose smut in barley occurred across Western Australia’s grain belt. Loose smut persists across seasons as dormant mycelium within infected seed, impacting both commercial and retained seed. In contrast, flag smut primarily spreads through contaminated soil. Despite seed treatments being the most effective control measure for these diseases, substantial outbreaks were reported by growers despite good seed dressing coverage and other hygiene practics.

The concentration of phosphine residue in grain post fumigation (where it is currently being measured) that poses no risk to workers is unknown. The SWA TLV-TWA is soon to be reduced to 0.05 ppm. Continuing current practices could result in the loss of phosphine as a registered stored grain fumigant and there is an urgent need to optimise post-fumigation protocols. This investment will address this by delivering: * Data packages required to update the phosphine label registration with the APVMA, including appropriate ventilation and withholding periods to reduce phosphine residue in grain to thresholds that meet SWA worker exposure limits. * A new or updated Australian standard for phosphine fumigation, including an agreed protocol of how phosphine residue in grain should be measured at receival sites to meet the SWA TLV-TWA, and appropriate clearance thresholds. * An on-farm protocol for growers to measure phosphine residue prior to outturn, to ensure residues are below thresholds set in the above standard.
